metadata.scope: e_abyssinia (all baronies across k_abyssinia, k_adal, k_nubia, x_script_2942, and k_damot)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.vanilla_ck3_name: Exact English localisation string from CK3 titles_l_english.yml.
schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/standard English display name of the audited settlement or holding (stripped of key prefixes and parenthetical notes).
schema_notes.modern_name_note: Optional administrative parent, alternate designation, or native-script qualifier extracted from modern_name; null if none.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.anachronism_type: Mutually exclusive historicity category: attested_pre_867 | fictional_placeholder | post_867_eponym | renamed_post_867 | modern_anachronism | early_modern_foundation | high_late_medieval_attestation | unattested_indigenous_or_minor.
schema_notes.is_historical_at: Bookmark-keyed booleans {'867', '1066', '1178'}: true iff first_mention_year is known and <= that bookmark year.
schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation for the audited name (negative values = BCE; null if unattested).
schema_notes.first_mention_attestation: Summary of earliest documented textual or epigraphic attestation (or unattested status).
schema_notes.eponym: Structured eponym object {year, post_867, type, details} when named after a person, saint, ruler, deity, or dynasty/tribe; null otherwise.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or topographic_feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with form, language, language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5), and translation.
schema_notes.etymology_analysis: Linguistic and historical etymology of the audited barony name.
schema_notes.historical_names: List of distinct pre-867 attested names for the same site or immediate predecessor: [{name, native_script, language, attested_from, attested_to, source, relationship, notes}].
schema_notes.source_url: Primary reference URL (Wikipedia or regional historical encyclopedia), or null if unavailable.

b_wiqro.first_mention_attestation: Named in medieval Ge'ez sources (including 13th-century traditions of King Lalibela); first European visit recorded by Francisco Álvares in 1521 CE. While pre-Aksumite inscriptions (8th–6th century BCE) exist nearby, the toponym Wiqro/Wukro itself is not attested in writing by 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: hewn or carved (referring to rock-hewn monolithic churches)

b_wiqro.etymology_analysis: From Tigrinya/Ge'ez wuqro ('carved/hewn from rock', from root w-q-r), referring to the region's monolithic rock-hewn churches such as Wukro Chirkos.

b_qohaito.first_mention_attestation: Modern Tigrinya toponym Qohaito recorded when the ruins were located by Clements Markham in 1868 CE; the ancient Aksumite city on the plateau is attested earlier as Koloe.

morphemes.translation: highland plateau settlement name (modern designation of ancient Koloe)

b_qohaito.etymology_analysis: Modern Tigrinya name (ቆሓይቶ) for the archaeological plateau site between Aksum and Adulis, corresponding to classical Koloe.

historical_names.name: Koloe
historical_names.source: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (late 1st century CE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Aksumite city on the Qohaito plateau identified with Koloe in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea.

b_matara.first_mention_attestation: Although the archaeological site near Senafe was a major Dʿmt and Aksumite city (4th–8th centuries CE) with the pre-Aksumite Hawulti obelisk, the toponym Matara/Metera itself is attested in medieval Ge'ez hagiographic traditions rather than a dated contemporary written source by 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: historical settlement name of the Senafe plateau site

b_matara.etymology_analysis: Tigrinya/Ge'ez toponym Metera (መጠራ), also known locally as Balaw Kalaw; exact pre-medieval lexical etymology is uncertain.

b_intarta.first_mention_attestation: Historically attested as the province of Enderta (Inderta) from at least the restoration of the Solomonic dynasty in 1270 CE and in early 14th-century land grants (1305 and 1318–1319 CE).
b_intarta.etymology_analysis: Ge'ez/Tigrinya provincial name Enderta (እንደርታ), historically linked to the salt-caravan trade between the Tigray highlands and the Danakil lowlands.

b_qiha.first_mention_attestation: While Aksumite ruins exist on nearby Kwiha Cherqos hill, the town name Kwiha (Quiha) is first described in the early 19th century CE by Nathaniel Pearce.
b_qiha.etymology_analysis: From the local Tigrinya word for willows, which grow abundantly along the stream near the town.

b_seraye.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the early 13th century CE in a land grant of Zagwe King Lalibela at Debre Libanos near Senafe, and later in the 16th-century Futuh al-Habasha (1535 CE).

morphemes.translation: highland province name (cognate with South Arabian Sarwān/Sarāt)

b_seraye.etymology_analysis: Ge'ez/Tigrinya provincial name Serae/Seraye (ሰራየ), compared by historians to South Arabian highland toponyms such as Sarwān and Sarāt.

b_hamasen.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 4th century CE (c. 350 CE) as the region ḤMS²M (ḤMŠ) in a Sabaic inscription of the Aksumite King Ezana.
b_hamasen.etymology_analysis: From ancient Sabaic/Aksumite ḤMS²M attested in King Ezana's 4th-century CE inscription, continuing as Ge'ez/Tigrinya Hamasien (ሐማሴን).

b_shimazana.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation by 867 CE; attested in later medieval and modern Eritrean highland and Saho historical records as a district of Akele Guzai.
b_shimazana.etymology_analysis: Regional toponym in southern Akele Guzai (Eritrea) along the Tigrinya-Saho linguistic borderland; pre-medieval etymology unattested.

b_aksum.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the mid-1st century CE (c. 60 CE) as the 'metropolis' of Auxoumis (Aksum) in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea.

morphemes.translation: capital city of the Aksumite Empire

b_aksum.etymology_analysis: Ancient Ge'ez toponym Aksum (አክሱም), recorded in Greek as Auxoumis in the 1st-century CE Periplus of the Erythraean Sea.

b_south_seraye.first_mention_attestation: No historical attestation by 867 CE; modern English directional subdivision ('South' + 'Seraye') created for game geography.
b_south_seraye.etymology_analysis: Modern English directional compound combining 'South' with the Eritrean provincial name Seraye.

b_tigre.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a 10th-century CE gloss to the 6th-century Christian Topography of Cosmas Indicopleustes as 'Tigrētai' (the tribes near Adulis).

morphemes.translation: northern Ethiopian highland ethnonym and province

b_tigre.etymology_analysis: Originally an ethnonym ('Tigrētai' in the 10th-century Cosmas Indicopleustes gloss) designating coastal/highland groups near Adulis, later applied to Tigray Province.

b_waldabba.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the late 14th century CE with the foundation of Waldebba Monastery by Saint Samuel of Waldebba (fl. late 14th–early 15th century CE).

morphemes.translation: monastic wilderness region in western Tigray

b_waldabba.etymology_analysis: Ge'ez/Tigrinya toponym Waldebba (ዋልድባ), associated with the major Ethiopian Orthodox monastic center established in the late 14th century CE.

b_joha.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation by 867 CE; unattested in standard historical and encyclopedic sources for Tigray.

morphemes.translation: unattested local holding name in Tigray

b_joha.etymology_analysis: Unattested in historical Ethiopian sources; etymology unknown.

b_buri.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation of the peninsula name Buri by 867 CE; the nearby mainland/regional name Bur is attested in medieval Ethiopian hagiographies and chronicles.

morphemes.translation: Red Sea peninsula east of the Gulf of Zula

b_buri.etymology_analysis: Topographic name of the Buri Peninsula jutting into the Red Sea between the Gulf of Zula and Howakil Bay, related to the regional name Bur.

b_bur.first_mention_attestation: Attested in medieval Ge'ez hagiographies (e.g., Gadla Aregawi, Gadla Sadqan, composed c. 14th–15th century CE, though recounting 6th-century CE traditions of King Kaleb) and 15th-century royal chronicles.

morphemes.translation: coastal and highland province across the Ethio-Eritrean border

b_bur.etymology_analysis: Ge'ez/Tigrinya historical province name Bur (ቡር), divided into Upper Bur (Akele Guzai/Agame) and Lower Bur (coastal lowlands).

b_saho.first_mention_attestation: First written mention appears in the Royal Chronicle of Emperor Susenyos I (r. 1606–1632 CE), noting a 'country of the Sahos' on the confines of the Ethiopian kingdom.

morphemes.translation: ethnonym of the Cushitic pastoralist people of Eritrea

b_saho.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym of the Saho people (often glossed in local tradition from saa 'livestock' + hoo 'caretaker', i.e., pastoralist/nomad).

b_dahlak_kebir.first_mention_attestation: The Dahlak Islands are attested in early Islamic historical sources from the Umayyad occupation of 702 CE (under Caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan), and in 9th–10th century Arabic geographies.
b_dahlak_kebir.etymology_analysis: Arabic Dahlak al-Kabīr ('Great Dahlak'), combining the pre-867 island name Dahlak (attested from 702 CE) with Arabic kabīr ('great') to distinguish the largest island.

historical_names.name: Alalaiou
historical_names.source: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (late 1st century CE)
historical_names.notes: Identified by G.W.B. Huntingford with the Alalaiou islands near Adulis described in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea.

b_gimhile.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation by 867 CE; unattested in standard historical and encyclopedic sources.

morphemes.translation: unattested local holding name in the Dahlak region

b_gimhile.etymology_analysis: Unattested in historical sources; etymology unknown.

b_massawa.first_mention_attestation: Although Massawa emerged as a port between the 8th and 10th centuries CE, the name Massawa (Mitsiwa) is attested in medieval Ethiopian sources such as the war songs of Emperor Yeshaq I (r. 1414–1429 CE).
b_massawa.etymology_analysis: Tigre/Ge'ez Mitsiwa (ምጽዋ), Arabic Maṣawwaʿ; traditionally associated with the coastal trading settlement on Basé and Taulud islands.

historical_names.name: Badi
historical_names.source: Early Islamic / Arab Red Sea trade records (c. 600–1100 CE, cited by Richard Pankhurst)
historical_names.notes: Richard Pankhurst identifies Massawa as the site of the earlier Arab Red Sea port of Badi (c. 600–1100 CE).

b_dehono.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the early 16th century CE (1513 CE Portuguese arrival at Arkiko/Dokono); earlier written attestation by 867 CE is lacking.
b_dehono.etymology_analysis: Historical name Dokono/Dakhano for Hergigo (Arkiko), derived from the Saho/Afar word for 'elephant' due to its role in the ivory trade.

b_berta.first_mention_attestation: The Berta people are attested from the 16th–17th centuries CE following their migration from the Funj Sultanate in Sennar to western Ethiopia.
b_berta.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym of the Nilo-Saharan-speaking Berta people of the Ethio-Sudanese borderlands (also called Bela Shangul / Benishangul).

b_abbay-agaw.first_mention_attestation: No historical attestation by 867 CE; modern historiographical/geographical compound combining the Abbay (Blue Nile) river and the Agaw people.

morphemes.translation: Central Cushitic ethnic group of northwestern Ethiopia

b_abbay-agaw.etymology_analysis: Compound of Abbay (the Ethiopian name for the Blue Nile) and Agaw (the Cushitic-speaking people of northwestern Ethiopia).

b_gambo.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 16th-century CE Ethiopian royal chronicles (e.g., Emperor Gelawdewos, r. 1540–1559 CE, suppressed a revolt in Gambo province).

morphemes.translation: historical Gafat clan and province name

b_gambo.etymology_analysis: Name of a historical Gafat clan and province south of the Blue Nile attested in 16th-century Solomonic chronicles.

b_bosha.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the early 15th century CE (reign of Emperor Yeshaq I, r. 1414–1429 CE) as the Kingdom of Garo/Bosha, a tributary state in the Gibe region.

morphemes.translation: ruling dynasty and kingdom name in the Gibe region

b_bosha.etymology_analysis: Name of the ruling dynasty of the Kingdom of Garo (also called Bosha) on the periphery of the Gibe region.

b_gurage.first_mention_attestation: First appears in the 14th-century CE Royal Chronicle of Emperor Amda Seyon I (r. 1314–1344 CE), which mentions a governor appointed for Alamalé in the 'Guragé country'.

morphemes.translation: ethnonym and highland region southwest of Addis Ababa

b_gurage.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym and regional name Gurage (ጉራጌ) first attested in 14th-century Solomonic chronicles.

b_bizamo.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the early 15th century CE as a tributary territory between the Abbay and Didessa rivers paying tribute in cotton cloth.
b_bizamo.etymology_analysis: Medieval polity located in the bend of the Abbay (Blue Nile) river, attested in 15th–17th century Ethiopian and Jesuit accounts.

b_jibat.first_mention_attestation: Attested in late 19th-century CE Shewan administration (granted alongside Mecha to Fitawrari Habte Giyorgis in 1897 CE); no written attestation by 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: district and mountain forest area in West Shewa

b_jibat.etymology_analysis: Toponym in West Shewa (Oromia, Ethiopia); unattested in pre-modern written sources.

b_damot-west.first_mention_attestation: No historical attestation by 867 CE; modern English directional subdivision ('Damot' + 'West') created for game geography.
b_damot-west.etymology_analysis: Modern English directional compound combining the medieval kingdom name Damot (formed c. 10th century CE) with 'West'.

b_innarya.first_mention_attestation: Recorded in the 13th century CE as a province of the Kingdom of Damot (and by the early 15th century CE as a tributary of Yeshaq I); 9th-century traditions of Digna-Jan's campaign are later oral accounts.

morphemes.translation: kingdom name in the Gibe region

b_innarya.etymology_analysis: From Gonga Hinnario (rendered in Amharic/Ge'ez as Ennarea/Innarya), the leading kingdom of the Gibe region from the 14th to 17th centuries CE.

b_gibe_innarya.first_mention_attestation: Compound of Gibe (first attested in the 1566 CE Royal Chronicle of Emperor Sarsa Dengel) and Innarya (13th century CE); unattested as a compound by 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: major tributary of the Omo River

b_gibe_innarya.etymology_analysis: Geographical compound combining the Gibe River with the historical kingdom of Innarya (Ennarea).

b_gomma.first_mention_attestation: Emerged as an Oromo kingdom in the Gibe region in the late 18th century CE (c. 1780–1800 CE); no written attestation by 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: Gibe region kingdom and woreda name

b_gomma.etymology_analysis: Name of one of the five Oromo monarchies of the Gibe region, founded in the late 18th century CE.

b_didesa.first_mention_attestation: First documented usage of the river name Didessa dates to 1861 CE (Antoine d'Abbadie's inquiries in Western Shoa, noted by Herbert Weld Blundell).

morphemes.translation: major western tributary of the Abbay (Blue Nile)

b_didesa.etymology_analysis: Oromo hydronym Dhedheessa for the major tributary of the Blue Nile in western Ethiopia, first recorded in 1861 CE.

b_wellega-south.first_mention_attestation: No historical attestation by 867 CE; modern English directional subdivision ('Wellega' + 'South') created for game geography.

morphemes.translation: western Ethiopian province named after the Wollega Oromo

b_wellega-south.etymology_analysis: Modern English directional compound combining the Oromo provincial name Wellega (Wallaggaa) with 'South'.

b_wellega-north.first_mention_attestation: No historical attestation by 867 CE; modern English directional subdivision ('Wellega' + 'North') created for game geography.

morphemes.translation: western Ethiopian province named after the Wollega Oromo

b_wellega-north.etymology_analysis: Modern English directional compound combining the Oromo provincial name Wellega (Wallaggaa) with 'North'.

b_agaw_meder.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 18th-century CE accounts (e.g., James Bruce, 1790 CE) as Agawmeder, the Agaw-inhabited district southwest of Gojjam.
b_agaw_meder.etymology_analysis: Amharic Agäw Mədər ('Land of the Agaw'), designating the Awi Agaw territory west of Gojjam.

b_upper_dinder.first_mention_attestation: No historical attestation by 867 CE; modern English directional hydronym ('Upper' + 'Dinder') for the headwaters of the Dinder River.

morphemes.translation: tributary river of the Blue Nile

b_upper_dinder.etymology_analysis: Modern English directional hydronym referring to the Ethiopian highland headwaters of the Dinder River.

b_dinder.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 18th century CE (Battle of the Dindar River in 1744 CE between Emperor Iyasu II and Sennar); first visited by Europeans in 1861 CE.

morphemes.translation: right-bank tributary of the Blue Nile

b_dinder.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Dinder River (Arabic Nahr al-Dindir, Amharic Dinder Wenz), rising in the Ethiopian highlands west of Lake Tana.

b_gafat.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the late 13th and 14th centuries CE (1270 CE support for Yekuno Amlak and 14th-century chronicles of Emperor Amda Seyon I).

morphemes.translation: extinct South Ethiopic group along the Blue Nile (postulated from Harari gáfá 'slave')

b_gafat.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym and region of the extinct Semitic-speaking Gafat people along the Blue Nile; linguists (cited by Giorgio Banti) have linked it to Harari gáfá.

b_west_gojjam.first_mention_attestation: No historical attestation by 867 CE; modern English directional subdivision ('West' + 'Gojjam') created for game geography.
b_west_gojjam.etymology_analysis: Modern English directional compound combining 'West' with the historical Ethiopian province name Gojjam.

b_gojjam.first_mention_attestation: Earliest recorded mention is in a manuscript note of Emperor Amda Seyon I's campaigns in Gojjam and Damot in 1309 EC (1316–1317 CE).

morphemes.translation: historical provincial kingdom within the Blue Nile bend

b_gojjam.etymology_analysis: Amharic Gojjam (ጎጃም), originally written Gʷazzam (ጐዛም) and later Gʷažžām, first attested in 1316–1317 CE.

b_bad.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation by 867 CE; unattested in standard historical and encyclopedic sources for Gojjam.

morphemes.translation: unattested local holding name in Gojjam

b_bad.etymology_analysis: Unattested in historical Ethiopian sources; etymology unknown.

b_bahir_giyorgis.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Bahir Giyorgis (the original settlement name of Bahir Dar, named after the St. George church on Lake Tana) is associated in Ethiopian tradition with the late 13th-century reign of Yekuno Amlak (r. 1270–1285 CE) and documented by 19th-century European travelers.

morphemes.translation: sea / large lake (referring to Lake Tana)

b_bahir_giyorgis.etymology_analysis: Amharic/Ge'ez compound meaning 'Sea/Lake George', referring to the church of St. George (Giyorgis) on the southern shore of Lake Tana, which gave its name to the early settlement before it was known as Bahir Dar.

b_warq.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Debre Werq (Däbrä Wärq) in Gojjam is first attested in 1559 CE during the reign of Emperor Gelawdewos, who supervised its restoration, and later in a 1684 CE itinerary of Emperor Iyasu I.

morphemes.translation: gold (shortened form of Däbrä Wärq, 'Mount of Gold')

b_warq.etymology_analysis: From Amharic/Ge'ez wärq ('gold'), representing the monastic settlement and town of Debre Werq ('Mount of Gold') in East Gojjam.

b_dima.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; the monastery of Dima (Dima Giyorgis) in Gojjam is attested in the chronicle of Emperor Susenyos for 1607 CE as the refuge of Ras Antenatewos after the Battle of Gol.

morphemes.translation: local toponym of Dima in East Gojjam

b_dima.etymology_analysis: Toponym of the historic town and monastery of Dima Giyorgis in East Gojjam, likely of local Agaw or Amharic origin.

b_begemdir.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; the earliest recorded mention of Begemder (Begemdir) is on the Fra Mauro world map (c. 1460 CE), where it is depicted as a kingdom.

morphemes.translation: sheep or dry-season pastoral land (uncertain first element)

b_begemdir.etymology_analysis: Amharic/Ge'ez compound Bägē-mədər (በጌምድር), conventionally interpreted as 'land of sheep' (from bäg, sheep) or 'land of Bega', designating the historic highland province east of Lake Tana.

b_belasa.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Belasa (Belesa) is a district and intermittent stream east of Gondar attested only in modern/early-modern sources.

morphemes.translation: local district name east of Gondar (cf. bäläs, fig/cactus)

b_belasa.etymology_analysis: Amharic toponym Bäläsa (Belesa), designating a district and river valley east of Gondar in historic Begemder.

b_sana.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Sana (Säna) in Begemder is unattested in pre-867 CE written sources and appears only in later/modern records.
b_sana.etymology_analysis: Local Ethiopian toponym in Begemder, unattested in early written sources.

b_gouzara.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; the royal castle of Guzara (Gouzara) near Emfraz in Begemder is dated to c. 1560–1572 CE under Emperor Minas or Emperor Sarsa Dengel.

morphemes.translation: hilltop royal palace site near Emfraz

b_gouzara.etymology_analysis: Amharic toponym Guzara (Gouzara), naming the 16th-century royal fortress site overlooking Lake Tana near Emfraz.

b_kibran.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Kebran Gabriel (Kibran) island monastery on Lake Tana was established in the 14th century CE and rebuilt under Emperor Iyasu I (1682–1706 CE).
b_kibran.etymology_analysis: Toponym of Kibran (Kebran) Island on Lake Tana, associated with Ge'ez kəbr ('honor, glory') and housing the 14th-century monastery of Kebran Gabriel.

b_gondar.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Gondar was founded as the permanent imperial capital of Ethiopia by Emperor Fasilides in 1636 CE.

morphemes.translation: imperial capital city founded on the ridge north of Lake Tana

b_gondar.etymology_analysis: Amharic Gondär (formerly Gʷändär), likely of local Cushitic (Agaw/Qemant) origin; established as Ethiopia's permanent capital by Emperor Fasilides in 1636 CE.

b_dembiya.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Dembiya is first mentioned in the Amharic soldiers' songs of Emperor Yeshaq I (r. 1414–1429 CE).

morphemes.translation: historic province north of Lake Tana

b_dembiya.etymology_analysis: Regional toponym Dämbiya (Dembiya) for the fertile plain on the northern shore of Lake Tana, attested from the 15th century CE.

b_galila.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Bahir Galila (Galila monastery on Lake Tana) dates to the medieval monastic expansion around Lake Tana in the 14th–16th centuries CE.

morphemes.translation: Galilee (biblical sacred name applied to the Lake Tana island monastery)

b_galila.etymology_analysis: Ge'ez Gälīla, derived from biblical Galilee and applied to the island monastery of Bahir Galila on the northern shore of Lake Tana.

b_kosoge.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Kosoge (Kossoye) north of Gondar is attested in Ethiopian royal chronicles for January 1781 CE.
b_kosoge.etymology_analysis: Amharic toponym Kosoge (Kossoye), meaning 'place/land of kosso trees' (Hagenia abyssinica), situated on the escarpment north of Gondar.

b_semien.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the 3rd–4th century CE Aksumite Greek inscription Monumentum Adulitanum (preserved by Cosmas Indicopleustes, c. 547–550 CE), describing the snow-covered mountains of the Semēnoi (Simien).
b_semien.etymology_analysis: From Ge'ez Səmen (recorded in Greek as Semēnoi in Monumentum Adulitanum), denoting the high mountain massif southwest of Aksum; the directional sense shifted from 'south' to 'north' as the Ethiopian political center moved southward.

b_falasha.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; the term Falasha (Ge'ez/Amharic fälaša) was applied to the Beta Israel community from the 15th century CE under Emperor Yeshaq I (r. 1414–1429 CE) and appears in 15th-century Jewish texts.
b_falasha.etymology_analysis: From Ge'ez root fäläsä ('to emigrate, wander, be exiled'), an exonym given to the Beta Israel (Ethiopian Jews) in the 15th century CE.

b_amhara.first_mention_attestation: No documented contemporaneous written attestation <= 867 CE; the earliest extant written record is the Arabic Chronicle of the Sultanate of Showa (recording a 1128 CE conflict with the Amhara in Warjih), followed by Umara al-Yamani (mid-12th century CE). Later 13th/14th-century hagiographies retroject the region to the 9th century.
b_amhara.etymology_analysis: Traditionally derived from Ge'ez ʿam ḥara ('free people' or 'soldiers'), denoting the core highland region (Bete Amhara) and ethnonym.

b_east_amhara.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; 'East Amhara' is a modern/in-game directional subdivision of Amhara (itself first contemporaneously attested in 1128 CE).

morphemes.translation: core Ethiopian highland region (from ʿam ḥara)

b_east_amhara.etymology_analysis: Modern English directional compound ('East' + Amhara) created to represent the eastern part of the medieval Amhara province.

b_wagda.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Wagda (Wegda) is attested in 14th-century Ethiopian monastic accounts of the evangelization of Shewa under Bishop Yaqob and Emperor Amda Seyon I (c. 1330s CE).

morphemes.translation: historic district in northern Shewa / southern Amhara

b_wagda.etymology_analysis: Amharic regional toponym Wägda (Wagda/Wegda), denoting a historic district bordering Tegulet and Bete Amhara.

b_walaqa.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; the Walaqa River and historic province of Walaqa (Wäläqa) are attested in 16th-century chronicles such as Futuh al-Habasha (1531 CE) and Solomonic royal records.

morphemes.translation: tributary river of the Blue Nile (Abay) and adjacent province

b_walaqa.etymology_analysis: Hydronym and provincial name Wäläqa (Walaqa), designating a major tributary of the Blue Nile between Amhara and Shewa.

b_angot.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Angot is attested in early Solomonic sources from the reign of Emperor Amda Seyon I (r. 1314–1344 CE) as a major province east of Lasta.

morphemes.translation: historic highland province between Tigray and Amhara

b_angot.etymology_analysis: Medieval Ethiopian provincial toponym Angot, situated east of Lasta and north of Lake Hayq.

b_bashila.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; the Bashilo River (Bashila) is attested in 17th-century Ethiopian historiography (such as Hiob Ludolf's map and royal chronicles) as the boundary between Begemder and Amhara Sayint.

morphemes.translation: major eastern tributary of the Blue Nile (Abay)

b_bashila.etymology_analysis: Hydronym Bäšəlo (Bashilo/Bashila), naming the deep canyon river flowing into the Blue Nile between Begemder and Amhara.

b_gishe.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Gishen / Amba Geshen (Gishe) is associated in Ethiopian church records with the reign of Emperor Yekuno Amlak (r. 1270–1285 CE) and Emperor Zara Yaqob (15th century CE).

morphemes.translation: historic district and flat-topped mountain stronghold in Wollo/North Shewa

b_gishe.etymology_analysis: Amharic toponym Gəše (Gishe), corresponding to the historic highland district and pilgrimage site of Gishen.

b_hayq.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; while later tradition attributes a 9th-century church on Lake Hayq to Aksumite king Dil Na'od, the earliest documented written attestation of Dabra Hayq is the 13th-century monastic foundation of Iyasus Mo'a in 1248 CE.
b_hayq.etymology_analysis: From Amharic/Ge'ez ḥayq ('lake'), denoting both Lake Hayq in South Wollo and the famous island monastery of Hayq Estifanos.

b_dabahu.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Dabahu is unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.
b_dabahu.etymology_analysis: Local Ethiopian toponym unattested in early written records.

b_lalibela.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; originally known as Roha/Adefa, the town was renamed Lalibela after Zagwe King Gebre Mesqel Lalibela (r. c. 1181–1221 CE) following his death in the early 13th century CE.

eponym.details: Named after King Gebre Mesqel Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty (r. c. 1181–1221 CE), who commissioned the rock-hewn churches at the site originally called Roha/Adefa.

morphemes.translation: the bees recognize his sovereignty (royal personal name)

b_lalibela.etymology_analysis: Named after King Gebre Mesqel Lalibela (r. c. 1181–1221 CE), whose name is traditionally explained in Ge'ez/Agaw hagiography as 'the bees recognize his sovereignty'.

b_tekeze.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a 4th-century CE Aksumite inscription of King Ezana (c. 350 CE), which records a victory on the lower banks of the Tekezé River near 'the ford of Kemalke'.

morphemes.translation: river / major watercourse of northern Ethiopia

b_tekeze.etymology_analysis: Ge'ez/Tigrinya hydronym Täkkäze (Tekezé), one of the major northern tributaries of the Nile, attested in 4th-century CE Aksumite royal inscriptions.

b_lasta.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Lasta is attested as the core mountainous homeland of the Agaw Zagwe dynasty (traditionally founded c. 1137 CE) in medieval Ethiopian sources.

morphemes.translation: historic mountainous province in northern Ethiopia

b_lasta.etymology_analysis: Agaw/Amharic provincial toponym Lāstā (Lasta), the heartland of the medieval Zagwe dynasty.

b_adafa.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Adefa (Adafa, also called Roha) is attested in medieval Ethiopian historiography as the capital of the Zagwe dynasty (c. 1137–1270 CE).

morphemes.translation: capital settlement of the Zagwe dynasty (near Lalibela)

b_adafa.etymology_analysis: Agaw/Ge'ez toponym Adefa (Adafa), the medieval capital of the Zagwe dynasty near Roha/Lalibela.

b_doba.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; the Doba region bordering Angot and Lasta is attested in Ethiopian royal chronicles during the reign of Emperor Baeda Maryam I (r. 1468–1478 CE).

morphemes.translation: historic pastoralist region bordering Angot and Tigray

b_doba.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym and regional toponym Doba, denoting the medieval pastoralist people and territory northeast of Lasta and Angot.

b_fatagar.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Fatagar (Fätägar) is attested in 14th-century Solomonic chronicles under Amda Seyon I (1330s CE), the soldiers' songs of Yeshaq I (1412–1430 CE), and Fra Mauro's map (c. 1450 CE).
b_fatagar.etymology_analysis: Medieval Ethiopian provincial toponym Fätägar (Fatagar) along the Zeila trade corridor in southern Shewa.

b_sarmat.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Sarmat is a historical district of Bulga in Shewa attested only in later Ethiopian records.
b_sarmat.etymology_analysis: Amharic regional toponym Särmat (Sarmat) in historic Bulga, Shewa.

b_silalish.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Silalish (Tsilalish, an older name for Bulga in Shewa) is attested in the hagiography of Saint Tekle Haymanot (b. 1215 CE in Zorare, Silalish) and 14th-century evangelization records.

morphemes.translation: historic district in central Shewa (ancient name for Bulga)

b_silalish.etymology_analysis: Amharic/Ge'ez toponym Ṣəlaləš (Tsilalish/Silalish), the medieval name for the Bulga region of Shewa.

b_ifat.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Ifat (Awfat/Wafat) is first attested in the late 13th century CE when Sultan Umar Walashma established the Sultanate of Ifat and conquered Shewa in 1285 CE.

morphemes.translation: historic Muslim sultanate and region in eastern Shewa

b_ifat.etymology_analysis: Ethio-Semitic/Arabic toponym Ifāt (also Awfāt / Wafāt), naming the medieval Muslim sultanate on the eastern escarpment of Shewa.

b_warjih.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; the Warjih (Werjih) are first attested in the Arabic Chronicle of the Sultanate of Showa for 1128 CE, which records that the Amhara fled from the land of Werjih.

morphemes.translation: historic pastoralist community and territory in the Awash Valley / Ifat

b_warjih.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym and territorial name Wärǧəḥ (Warjih/Werjih), denoting a Muslim pastoralist group in eastern Shewa and the Awash Valley.

b_gidim.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Gidim (Gedem) is attested in 14th-century sources including Shihab al-Umari's Masalik al-absar (1340s CE) and the Chronicle of Amda Seyon I as a district of Ifat.

morphemes.translation: historic district of Ifat in northeastern Shewa

b_gidim.etymology_analysis: Regional toponym Gədəm (Gidim), one of the constituent districts of medieval Ifat in northeastern Shewa.

b_katata.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Katata (Ketata) in Shewa is attested in the hagiography of Saint Tekle Haymanot (13th–14th century CE) as a district he traversed during his mid-13th-century travels.

morphemes.translation: historic district on the Shewan plateau

b_katata.etymology_analysis: Amharic toponym Kätata (Katata), designating a medieval district in Shewa.

b_debre_libanos.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; founded in 1284 CE by Saint Tekle Haymanot as Debre Atsbo and renamed Debre Libanos in the 15th century CE.
b_debre_libanos.etymology_analysis: Ge'ez Däbrä Libanos ('Mount of Lebanon'), the 15th-century name given to the major Shewan monastery originally founded as Debre Atsbo in 1284 CE.

b_warab.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Warab (Wereb) in Shewa is attested in 14th-century hagiographical sources (such as the Life of Filpos and evangelization records under Bishop Yaqob, c. 1330s CE).
b_warab.etymology_analysis: Amharic regional toponym Wäräb (Warab/Wereb) in medieval Shewa.

b_mugar.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; the Muger River (Mugar) in Shewa is attested only in post-867 medieval and early modern sources.

morphemes.translation: tributary river of the Blue Nile in Shewa

b_mugar.etymology_analysis: Hydronym Mugär (Muger/Mugar), naming a major tributary of the Blue Nile in central Shewa.

b_indegabtan.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Indegabtan (Endagabtan) in Shewa is attested in Ge'ez Marian manuscripts (e.g., Miracles of Mary at Hagara Maryam, c. 1524 CE) during the reign of Emperor Lebna Dengel.
b_indegabtan.etymology_analysis: Medieval Ethiopian toponym ʾƎndägäbtan (Indegabtan), designating a historic district in Shewa.

b_waj.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Wej (Waj/Wäj) is a medieval province southwest of Shewa near Lake Zway, attested from the 12th century CE (1129 CE) and prominent in Solomonic chronicles from the 13th–16th centuries CE.

morphemes.translation: historic province near Lake Zway in southern Shewa

b_waj.etymology_analysis: Medieval Ethiopian provincial toponym Wäǧ (Waj/Wej), situated west of Fatagar near Lake Zway.

b_geberge.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Gabarge (Geberge) is attested in the 13th-century Chronicle of the Sultanate of Showa (in conflict with Dil Marrah, 1270s CE) and in 16th-century chronicles as a royal site in Wej where Emperor Lebna Dengel received news of the Adal invasion.
b_geberge.etymology_analysis: Amharic toponym Gäbärge (Geberge/Gabarge), a medieval settlement and royal camp in the province of Wej.

b_dakkar.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the early 15th century CE (c. 1415 CE) by Walashma ruler Sabr ad-Din III as the first capital of the Adal Sultanate.

morphemes.translation: historical Muslim town and first capital of the Adal Sultanate

b_dakkar.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Harari (Däkkär) and Somali (Doggor) toponym for the 15th-century Walashma capital east of Harar; exact lexical root is uncertain.

b_adal.first_mention_attestation: Earliest documented reference dates to July 1288 CE, when Walashma ruler Ali Baziyu campaigned in Adal and Mora following the collapse of the Makhzumi dynasty; also mentioned by Marco Polo in 1295 CE and by al-Umari in the 14th century CE.

morphemes.translation: historical Muslim region between Ifat, Harar, and Zeila

b_adal.etymology_analysis: Medieval regional name (Harari Aw Idal / Aw Abdal, Somali Awdal) attested from 1288 CE; later tradition links it to an 11th-century Emir Eidal or Aw Abdal, though its origin remains uncertain.

b_aw_barre.first_mention_attestation: Ruined Adal-era town and saint's shrine first recorded in Western literature by Richard Francis Burton in 1856 CE (as 'Ao Barhe' in First Footsteps in East Africa); flourished as an Adal Sultanate town in the 15th–16th centuries CE.

eponym.details: Named after Sheikh Aw Barre (Awbare), an Adal-era Muslim patron saint (post-867 CE) whose tomb lies just west of the town.

morphemes.translation: father, respected elder, or saintly honorific
personal name of the local patron saint

b_aw_barre.etymology_analysis: Compound of the Harari/Somali saintly honorific 'Aw' ('father, saint') and the personal name Barre, denoting the burial site of the Adal-era patron saint Sheikh Aw Barre.

b_harar.first_mention_attestation: First contemporary written attestation in the 14th-century Royal Chronicle of Emperor Amda Seyon I (1332 CE, as Gēt/Harar sending governors to support Salih at the Battle of Das); the semi-legendary Fath Madinat Harar also records Abadir Umar ar-Rida settling on the plateau c. 1216 CE.

morphemes.translation: walled city of the Harar plateau (possibly linked to the Harla ethnonym)

b_harar.etymology_analysis: Toponym of uncertain etymology; archaeologist Timothy Insoll suggests a connection to the Harla people, while local Harari speakers historically call the city Gēy ('the city').

b_west_adal.first_mention_attestation: Unattested synthetic directional barony name created for gameplay; no historical settlement or written attestation exists under the name 'West Adal'.

morphemes.translation: historical Muslim region of the Horn of Africa

b_west_adal.etymology_analysis: Modern English directional qualifier 'West' prefixed to the medieval regional name Adal (attested from 1288 CE).

b_jebel_ahmar.first_mention_attestation: The Ahmar Mountains (Arabic Jabal al-Ahmar, 'Red Mountain') in eastern Oromia near Harar were documented by Richard Francis Burton in January 1854 CE during his journey to Harar.
b_jebel_ahmar.etymology_analysis: Arabic oronym Jabal al-Aḥmar ('Red Mountain'), referring to the Ahmar Mountains range of eastern Ethiopia south of Dire Dawa and west of Harar.

b_hargaya.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the 14th century CE (1332 CE) in the Royal Chronicle of Emperor Amda Seyon I as a Muslim polity in Adal; later attested in Emperor Baeda Maryam I's chronicle (15th century CE) and the 16th-century Futuh al-Habasha.

morphemes.translation: medieval Harla sub-clan and Muslim district on the Harar plateau

b_hargaya.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Harari/Harla ethnonym and polity name (Harari: Härgāyä) for a medieval Muslim district in Adal.

b_hargaya-west.first_mention_attestation: Unattested synthetic directional barony name created for gameplay; no historical settlement or written attestation exists under the name 'Hargaya-West'.

morphemes.translation: medieval Muslim district on the Harar plateau

b_hargaya-west.etymology_analysis: Synthetic directional compound combining the medieval Harari/Harla polity name Hargaya (attested 1332 CE) with English 'West'.

b_hargaya-south.first_mention_attestation: Unattested synthetic directional barony name created for gameplay; no historical settlement or written attestation exists under the name 'Hargaya-South'.

morphemes.translation: medieval Muslim district on the Harar plateau

b_hargaya-south.etymology_analysis: Synthetic directional compound combining the medieval Harari/Harla polity name Hargaya (attested 1332 CE) with English 'South'.

b_afar.first_mention_attestation: Earliest surviving written mention of the Afar dates to the 13th century CE (c. 1250 CE) in the writings of the Andalusian Arab geographer Ibn Sa'id al-Maghribi, who placed them from Suakin to Bab-el-Mandeb.

morphemes.translation: endonym of the Afar people and their homeland

b_afar.etymology_analysis: East Cushitic endonym (ʿAfar) of the Afar people of the Horn of Africa, first attested in Arabic geographic literature in the 13th century CE.

b_south_danakil.first_mention_attestation: Unattested synthetic directional barony name created for gameplay; no historical settlement or written attestation exists under the name 'South Danakil'.

morphemes.translation: Arabic plural exonym (Danākil) for the Dankali/Afar region

b_south_danakil.etymology_analysis: Modern English directional qualifier 'South' prefixed to Danakil (Arabic plural of Dankali, attested from the 13th century CE).

b_north_afar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested synthetic directional barony name created for gameplay; no historical settlement or written attestation exists under the name 'North Afar'.

morphemes.translation: endonym of the Afar people and region

b_north_afar.etymology_analysis: Modern English directional qualifier 'North' prefixed to the East Cushitic ethnonym/choronym Afar.

b_amarta.first_mention_attestation: Mount Amarta (part of the Amarta-Barawli volcanic complex in the southern Danakil Depression) was documented in 1934 CE by explorer L. M. Nesbitt in his account of crossing the Danakil.

morphemes.translation: volcanic mountain on the southern edge of the Danakil Depression

b_amarta.etymology_analysis: Afar oronym for Mount Amarta in the southern Danakil Depression, unattested in writing prior to 20th-century exploration.

b_ragali.first_mention_attestation: The Ragali River (the only permanent stream feeding Lake Karum in the northern Danakil Depression) was recorded in 1867 CE by Swiss explorer Werner Munzinger during his expedition through the Afar country.

morphemes.translation: permanent river flowing into Lake Karum in the Danakil Depression

b_ragali.etymology_analysis: Afar hydronym for the Ragali (Awra) River draining into Lake Karum (Assale), first documented in 1867 CE.

b_afera.first_mention_attestation: Lake Afrera (Afera / Afdera) in the Danakil Depression was reached and documented by European explorers in 1881 CE (named Lake Giulietti after Giuseppe Maria Giulietti); no pre-modern written attestation exists.

morphemes.translation: hypersaline endorheic lake in the Danakil Depression

b_afera.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Afar hydronym for Lake Afrera (Afdera) in the Danakil Depression, unattested in writing before the late 19th century CE.

b_edd.first_mention_attestation: Earliest dated documentary record is the 12 September 1840 CE purchase contract between Sheikh Mahmud Hasan of Edd and Badri Ali and representatives of the French Compagnie Nanto-Bordelaise.

morphemes.translation: Red Sea coastal port town in southern Eritrea

b_edd.etymology_analysis: Afar coastal settlement name (ʿƎdd) on the southern Eritrean Red Sea littoral; unattested in writing prior to the 19th century CE.

b_edd-north.first_mention_attestation: Unattested synthetic directional barony name created for gameplay; no historical settlement or written attestation exists under the name 'Edd-North'.

morphemes.translation: Red Sea coastal port town in southern Eritrea

b_edd-north.etymology_analysis: Synthetic directional compound combining the Eritrean port name Edd (attested 1840 CE) with English 'North'.

b_arusi.first_mention_attestation: Arusi (Arsi) refers to the Arsi Oromo branch and region, which became established in southeastern Ethiopia during the late 16th and early 17th centuries CE (c. 1600 CE) following the Oromo migrations.

morphemes.translation: Oromo branch and historical highland province in southeastern Ethiopia

b_arusi.etymology_analysis: Oromo ethnonym and regional name (Arsi, historically rendered Arusi), emerging after the 16th-century Oromo expansion into the former Dawaro/Bale region.

b_boke.first_mention_attestation: No pre-modern written attestation found; Boke is a modern district (woreda) and settlement (Boke Tiko) in West Hararghe Zone, Oromia Region, Ethiopia.

morphemes.translation: district and town in West Hararghe (Oromo: boke/bookee, mosquito or local toponym)

b_boke.etymology_analysis: Modern Oromo district and town name in West Hararghe Zone, Ethiopia, with no medieval written attestation.

b_arusi-north.first_mention_attestation: Unattested synthetic directional barony name created for gameplay; no historical settlement or written attestation exists under the name 'Arusi-North'.

morphemes.translation: Oromo branch and historical Ethiopian province

b_arusi-north.etymology_analysis: Synthetic directional compound combining Arusi (Arsi) with English 'North'.

b_karayu.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in writing in 1593 CE by the Ethiopian monk Abba Bahrey in his History of the Galla (Zenahu le-Galla) during the 16th-century Oromo migrations.

morphemes.translation: pastoralist Oromo clan inhabiting the Middle Awash Valley

b_karayu.etymology_analysis: Oromo clan ethnonym (Karrayyu) of the Awash Valley, first attested in Abba Bahrey's 1593 CE chronicle.

b_dawaro.first_mention_attestation: Earliest written mention of Dawaro appears in the 14th-century Royal Chronicle of Emperor Amda Seyon I (1332 CE), who subjugated and garrisoned the Muslim principality; also described by al-Umari in the 1340s CE.

morphemes.translation: medieval Muslim principality and Ethiopian province east of Hadiya

b_dawaro.etymology_analysis: Medieval Ethio-Semitic/Harari polity name (Dawāro) for the principality between Hadiya and Bali, attested from 1332 CE.

b_dawaro-west.first_mention_attestation: Unattested synthetic directional barony name created for gameplay; no historical settlement or written attestation exists under the name 'Dawaro-West'.

morphemes.translation: medieval Muslim principality in southeastern Ethiopia

b_dawaro-west.etymology_analysis: Synthetic directional compound combining the medieval principality name Dawaro (attested 1332 CE) with English 'West'.

b_bate.first_mention_attestation: Arabic funerary stelae discovered at Bate (near Harar/Haramaya) are epigraphically dated to the late 11th to early 12th century CE (c. 1100 CE); no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: settlement near Harar and Haramaya in eastern Ethiopia

b_bate.etymology_analysis: Local Ethiopian toponym (Baté/Bate) near Harar, associated with medieval Arabic funerary inscriptions dated to c. 1100 CE.

b_gendebelo.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the early 16th century CE in Venetian traveler Alessandro Zorzi's Ethiopian itineraries (c. 1523 CE) and in the Futuh al-Habasha by Arab Faqih (1530s–1540s CE) as a major Muslim trading city in Ifat.

morphemes.translation: medieval Muslim mercantile city in Ifat

b_gendebelo.etymology_analysis: Medieval Ethiopian Muslim commercial town name (Gendebelo / Gendabelo, identified archaeologically with Nora in Ifat), attested in 16th-century sources.

b_gabal.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 14th-century Royal Chronicle of Emperor Amda Seyon I (1332 CE) alongside the Warjeh Muslim pastoralists of the Awash Valley under the Sultanate of Ifat (possibly linked to the Gbbah noted in the Shewa chronicle for 1108 CE).

morphemes.translation: medieval Muslim pastoralist community and district in Ifat

b_gabal.etymology_analysis: Medieval Ethiopian Muslim ethnonym/district name (Gabal, a sub-group associated with the Warjeh in the Awash Valley), attested in 14th-century chronicles.

b_gabal_south.first_mention_attestation: Unattested synthetic directional barony name created for gameplay; no historical settlement or written attestation exists under the name 'Gabal South'.

morphemes.translation: medieval Muslim pastoralist community and district in Ifat

b_gabal_south.etymology_analysis: Synthetic directional compound combining the medieval Ethiopian district name Gabal (attested 1332 CE) with English 'South'.

b_awssa.first_mention_attestation: 1576–1577 CE (Imamate of Aussa established when Muhammad Gasa moved the Adalite capital from Harar to Aussa, recorded in the late 16th-century Harari Arabic chronicle Ta'rikh al-muluk)

morphemes.translation: lowland oasis settlement in the lower Awash basin

b_awssa.etymology_analysis: Toponym of the Afar lowland oasis (rendered Aussa, Awsa, or Awssa) in the lower Awash River basin. First attested in written sources in the late 16th century CE (1576–1577 CE) when Imam Muhammad Gasa relocated the Adalite seat from Harar to Aussa.

b_mora-awssa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a compound; Mora is first attested in 1264 CE (Makhzumi conflict) and Aussa in 1576 CE, while Mora-Awssa is a modern/game hyphenated compound.

morphemes.translation: medieval Muslim polity north of Ifat

b_mora-awssa.etymology_analysis: A composite toponym joining medieval Mora (attested from 1264 CE in Makhzumi and Ifat chronicles) with Aussa (attested from 1576 CE). Neither component nor the compound is attested in writing by 867 CE.

b_awash.first_mention_attestation: 16th century CE (recorded as the Awash / Hawash / Great Dir river in 16th-century Ethiopian–Adal chronicles such as the Futuh al-Habash and Portuguese accounts)

morphemes.translation: major endorheic river of the Ethiopian Rift

b_awash.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Awash River (also spelled Hawash; Amharic Awaš, Oromo Awaash/Hawaas, Afar Hawaash We'ayot). Although the river valley is paleoanthropologically ancient, the river name itself is not attested in writing before the 16th century CE.

b_abbe.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; first documented in modern geographical and exploration accounts (e.g., Wilfred Thesiger's 1933–1934 CE expedition to Lake Abhe Bad).

morphemes.translation: hypersaline terminal lake of the Awash River

b_abbe.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of Lake Abbe (Lake Abhe Bad), the terminal hypersaline lake of the Awash River on the Ethiopia–Djibouti border. The toponym has no pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_sitti.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; Sitti is a modern Somali administrative zone name in Ethiopia (formerly Shinile Zone).

morphemes.translation: northernmost administrative zone of Ethiopia's Somali Region

b_sitti.etymology_analysis: Modern Somali regional toponym (Gobolka Sitti) adopted in the 21st century for the former Shinile Zone in eastern Ethiopia. It has no pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_middle_awash.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; Middle Awash is a modern English geographical and paleoanthropological designation for the middle reach of the Awash River Valley.
b_middle_awash.etymology_analysis: Modern English geographical designation combining the directional/positional modifier 'Middle' with the Awash River hydronym (itself unattested before the 16th century CE).

b_busaso.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; Bosaso (originally Bender Qassim) is attributed in local tradition to the 14th-century settlement of trader Qasim and his camel Boosaas.

morphemes.translation: town named after Qasim's camel Boosaas

b_busaso.etymology_analysis: From Somali Boosaaso, derived according to local tradition from Boosaas, the favorite camel of the 14th-century trader Qasim after whom the settlement was first called Bender Qassim. In classical antiquity, the vicinity was known as Mosylon.

historical_names.name: Mosylon
historical_names.source: 1st century CE (Periplus of the Erythraean Sea §10, Pliny the Elder's Natural History, and Dioscorides' De Materia Medica)
historical_names.notes: Classical Greco-Roman emporium and cinnamon port located at or near modern Bosaso.

historical_names.name: Mosyllon
historical_names.source: 1st century CE (Periplus of the Erythraean Sea §10, Pliny the Elder's Natural History, and Dioscorides' De Materia Medica)
historical_names.notes: Classical Greco-Roman emporium and cinnamon port located at or near modern Bosaso.

b_qumbucul.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; Qombo'ul (Qumbucul) contains undated archaeological ruins in eastern Sanaag without pre-867 written records.

morphemes.translation: historic ruined settlement in eastern Sanaag

b_qumbucul.etymology_analysis: Somali toponym Qumbucul (also spelled Qombo'ul) in eastern Sanaag, Somaliland. While the site preserves ancient stone ruins of obscure date, the name has no documented written attestation by 867 CE.

b_el-ayo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; El Ayo (Ceelaayo) is a coastal town near undated cairns and rock art in eastern Sanaag, lacking pre-867 written attestation.
b_el-ayo.etymology_analysis: From Somali Ceelaayo (anglicized El Ayo / El Ayum), combining ceel ('well') with aayo. Despite nearby prehistoric rock art (Karinhegane) and cairns, the toponym is unattested in writing before 867 CE.

b_mait.first_mention_attestation: 11th century CE (c. 1020–1050 CE, depicted as Maydh on the Indian Ocean map in the Fatimid Book of Curiosities; later noted by Ahmad ibn Majid in the 15th century CE)

morphemes.translation: coastal port town in eastern Sanaag

b_mait.etymology_analysis: From Somali Maydh (Arabic Mīṭ, European Mait/Meit), an ancient coastal port in eastern Sanaag. First attested in writing in the 11th-century Book of Curiosities (post-867 CE), and later associated with the 12th–13th century tomb of Sheikh Isaaq.

b_laas_qoray.first_mention_attestation: 1735 CE (modern town founded by Sheikh Ali Mohamud Nuh of the Warsangali clan, though the surrounding area was a Warsangali center from the 13th century CE)
b_laas_qoray.etymology_analysis: From Somali Laasqoray (Laas Qoray), combining laas ('shallow well') and qoray ('wood' or 'carved'). The port town was founded in 1735 CE and has no pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_haylan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; Haylan is an old settlement in eastern Sanaag with undated ruins and the traditional tomb of Sheikh Darod.

morphemes.translation: historic town and burial site in eastern Sanaag

b_haylan.etymology_analysis: Somali toponym Heylaan (Haylan) in eastern Sanaag, known for undated archaeological ruins and the tomb of Sheikh Darod. No written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.

b_makhir.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; Maakhir is a Somali/Arabic regional designation for the northern Somali coastal people and Warsangali territory.

morphemes.translation: the people on the coast (northern Somali littoral)

b_makhir.etymology_analysis: From Somali Maakhir (Arabic Mākhir), a regional term meaning 'the people on the coast' associated with the Warsangali Sultanate in eastern Sanaag and western Bari. It has no pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_sheikh.first_mention_attestation: Late 14th century CE (archaeological occupation of the medieval settlement Fardowsa at Sheikh dates to the 13th–15th centuries CE; the modern town name Sheikh reflects its Islamic religious heritage)
b_sheikh.etymology_analysis: From Somali Sheekh, borrowed from Arabic shaykh ('elder, Islamic scholar'). Associated with the medieval Adal-era caravan town of Fardowsa (13th–16th centuries CE); unattested before 867 CE.

b_togdheer.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; Togdheer is a Somali hydronym ('Long River') and modern administrative region.
b_togdheer.etymology_analysis: From Somali Togdheer, literally 'Long River' (tog 'seasonal river/wadi' + dheer 'long'), referring to the Togdheer River and the surrounding region in Somaliland. Unattested in writing before 867 CE.

b_berbera.first_mention_attestation: 12th century CE (city of Berbera/Barbara recorded by Arab geographer al-Idrisi in 1154 CE; earlier classical/early medieval references to Barbaria and Po-pa-li denoted the broader Somali coast rather than the specific city)

morphemes.translation: port city of the Barbar coast (also folk-etymologized in Somali from beri-beri 'occasionally')

b_berbera.etymology_analysis: Derives from the Greco-Roman and Arabic regional name Barbaria / Bilad al-Barbar (and in Somali folk etymology from beri-beri, 'occasionally', referring to seasonal habitation). While the coast was called Barbaria from antiquity, Berbera as a city name is attested from the 12th century CE; in the 1st century CE the port was known as Malao.

historical_names.name: Malao
historical_names.source: 1st century CE (Periplus of the Erythraean Sea §8)
historical_names.notes: Classical Greek name for the ancient port city positioned at the site of modern Berbera.

b_amud.first_mention_attestation: c. 13th century CE (archaeological origins of the Ifat–Adal ruined town dated to around the 13th century CE; later described by Richard F. Burton in the 19th century)

eponym.details: Named after patron Saint Amud (Aw Amud), a local Muslim saint buried near the 13th-century Ifat–Adal town.

morphemes.translation: personal name of patron Saint Amud (Arabic ʿAmūd 'pillar')

b_amud.etymology_analysis: Named after its patron saint, Saint Amud (Somali Camuud, Arabic ʿAmūd), who is buried near the ruins of the 13th-century Ifat–Adal town southeast of Borama. No pre-867 CE attestation exists.

b_gogesa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; Gogesa (Dirbi Gogesa / Gogaysa) is a medieval ruined settlement in Woqooyi Galbeed first documented by modern archaeologists such as A. T. Curle (1937 CE).

morphemes.translation: medieval ruined settlement in Woqooyi Galbeed

b_gogesa.etymology_analysis: Somali toponym Gogesa (Gogaysa, also Dirbi Gogesa where dirbi denotes 'wall/ruins'), designating one of the major medieval ruined towns of western Somaliland. Unattested in writing before 867 CE.

b_tadjoura.first_mention_attestation: Early 19th century CE (c. 1810 CE, following the Adoimara Afar victory over the Asa-yamara; Mordechai Abir notes the port is absent from 18th-century Red Sea records)
b_tadjoura.etymology_analysis: From Afar Tagórri (Arabic Tājūrāʾ, French Tadjoura), derived from *tagór-li ('that which has goatskin water flasks', i.e., 'abundant with water'). Unattested before the early 19th century CE.

b_assab.first_mention_attestation: 1869 CE (Bay of Assab purchased by Giuseppe Sapeto for the Rubattino Shipping Company, and founded as a port in 1882 CE; previously a small Afar fishing village)

morphemes.translation: Red Sea coastal port in southern Eritrea

b_assab.etymology_analysis: Coastal toponym of southern Eritrea (Tigrinya ʿAsäb, Arabic ʿAṣab). Unattested before the 19th century CE, when the Bay of Assab was purchased in 1869 CE and developed into an Italian port in 1882 CE.

b_awbuk.first_mention_attestation: 1862 CE (treaty signed between France and local Afar rulers on 11 March 1862 CE establishing the French coaling station at Obock)

morphemes.translation: name of a local wadi near the port of Obock

b_awbuk.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Oboh (French Obock, game Awbuk), deformed from Afar Oboki, the name of a local wadi. Unattested in writing before the 19th century CE.

b_zaila.first_mention_attestation: Late 9th century CE (872–891 CE, first attested as Zaylaʿ in the Arabic geographical and historical works of al-Ya'qubi as capital of the early Adal kingdom)

morphemes.translation: historic Red Sea/Gulf of Aden port city

b_zaila.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Zaylaʿ (Somali Saylac, anglicized Zeila/Zaila). First attested in writing in the late 9th century CE by al-Ya'qubi (just after the 867 CE baseline), while the classical 1st-century CE port at or near the site was called Avalites.

historical_names.name: Avalites
historical_names.source: 1st century CE (Periplus of the Erythraean Sea §7 and Claudius Ptolemy's Geography)
historical_names.notes: Classical Greco-Roman emporium widely identified with the site of Zeila.

historical_names.name: Aualites
historical_names.source: 1st century CE (Periplus of the Erythraean Sea §7 and Claudius Ptolemy's Geography)
historical_names.notes: Classical Greco-Roman emporium widely identified with the site of Zeila.

b_abasa.first_mention_attestation: 16th–17th century CE (described as 'Abaxa, the Capital City of the Kingdom of Adel' in Portuguese Jesuit accounts; archaeological remains include 14th–16th century CE Islamic pottery)

morphemes.translation: ruined medieval Adal city in Awdal

b_abasa.etymology_analysis: Somali toponym Abaaso (Abasa / Abbasa), a major ruined town of the Adal Sultanate in Awdal, Somaliland. Archaeological finds date to the 14th–16th centuries CE and written mentions begin with early modern Portuguese Jesuit accounts.

b_ghoubet.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; Ghoubbet-el-Kharab ('the Gulf of the Demons') is an Arabic hydrographic name recorded in modern exploration.
b_ghoubet.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Qubbat al-Kharāb (French Ghoubbet-el-Kharab, 'Gulf of the Demons' or 'Cove of Ruin'), a deep volcanic cove at the western end of the Gulf of Tadjoura in Djibouti. Unattested in writing before 867 CE.

b_fafan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; Fafan is a Somali hydronym and modern administrative zone in Ethiopia's Somali Region.

morphemes.translation: seasonal river and basin in eastern Ethiopia

b_fafan.etymology_analysis: Somali hydronym Faafan (Fafan River), a tributary of the Shabelle/Jubba drainage system that also names the modern Fafan Zone in eastern Ethiopia. No pre-867 CE written attestation exists.

b_hargeisa.first_mention_attestation: Latter half of the 19th century CE (founded c. 1860s–1880s CE as a Qadiriyya settlement by Sheikh Madar Shirwa; described by H. G. C. Swayne in the 1880s–1890s CE)

morphemes.translation: from hargageys ('place to sell hides and skins') or Harar as-saghir ('Little Harar')

b_hargeisa.etymology_analysis: From Somali Hargeysa, either from hargageys ('place to sell hides and skins') or from Arabic Harar al-ṣaghīr ('Little Harar'), named by its 19th-century founder Sheikh Madar Shirwa. Unattested before the 19th century CE.

b_fafan-south.first_mention_attestation: Unattested before 867 CE; Fafan-South is a modern English directional compound designating the southern reach of the Fafan River valley.
b_fafan-south.etymology_analysis: Modern English directional compound combining the Somali Fafan River hydronym with 'South'. Neither the river name nor the compound is attested in writing by 867 CE.

b_gamo.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written records in the 15th century CE in the Ge'ez royal praise songs of Emperor Yeshaq I (r. 1413–1430 CE); no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_gamo.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym and toponym of the Gamo people of the Gamo Highlands in southern Ethiopia; in the Gamo language, 'gaammo' means 'lion'.

b_omo.first_mention_attestation: First documented in European written records during Italian explorer Vittorio Bottego's expedition to the river in 1896 CE (later also called Omo-Bottego); no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: river name (southern Ethiopian river emptying into Lake Turkana)

b_omo.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Omo River in southern Ethiopia, the largest Ethiopian river outside the Nile Basin and eponym of the Omotic language family.

b_lower_omo.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; 'Lower Omo' is a modern geographical designation for the lower delta valley of the Omo River (explored and mapped in 1896–1899 CE).
b_lower_omo.etymology_analysis: Modern English geographical descriptor combining 'Lower' with the Omo River hydronym to denote the lower valley and delta near Lake Turkana.

b_bonga.first_mention_attestation: Associated with the Kingdom of Kaffa (founded c. 1390 CE), with first recorded European mention by Antoine Thomson d'Abbadie in 1843 CE; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: historic capital town of the Kingdom of Kaffa

b_bonga.etymology_analysis: Toponym of the historic first capital of the Kingdom of Kaffa in southwestern Ethiopia, traditionally linked to founder/ruler Bon-noghe.

b_kaffa.first_mention_attestation: The Kingdom of Kaffa was founded c. 1390 CE according to oral tradition, and is first attested in written historical records in the 16th century CE (reign of Emperor Sarsa Dengel, 1563–1597 CE); no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: highland kingdom and ethnic region in southwestern Ethiopia

b_kaffa.etymology_analysis: Toponym and ethnonym of the Kafa (Kefficho) people and Kingdom of Kaffa in southwestern Ethiopia, famed as a center of wild Arabica coffee.

b_welamo.first_mention_attestation: The Kingdom of Wolaita (historically also rendered Welamo / Wollamo) was founded c. 1251 CE according to dynastic tradition and is attested in medieval Ethiopian records from the 13th–16th centuries CE; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: historic Amharic exonym for the Wolayta people and kingdom

b_welamo.etymology_analysis: Welamo is the historical Amharic/external rendering of Wolayta (Wolaitta), an Omotic-speaking people and medieval kingdom in southern Ethiopia.

b_gojeb.first_mention_attestation: Served as the northern defensive frontier of the Kingdom of Kaffa (16th–19th centuries CE) and was documented by Russian officer Alexander Bulatovich in January 1897 CE; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: river name (major right-bank tributary of the Omo River)

b_gojeb.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Gojeb River in southwestern Ethiopia, flowing eastward from the Guma Mountains into the Omo River.

b_janjero.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written records in a Ge'ez victory song of Emperor Yeshaq I (r. 1413–1430 CE) as a tributary state south of the Abay River; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: historical exonym for the Kingdom of Yamma (Yem)

b_janjero.etymology_analysis: Janjero is the historical Amharic exonym for the Omotic Kingdom of Yamma (Yem) in southwestern Ethiopia, located between the Omo and Jimma Gibe rivers.

b_welamo-west.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; 'Welamo-West' is a modern directional in-game sub-barony designation (paired with fictional/anachronistic 'Landolfstat' in the repository).
b_welamo-west.etymology_analysis: Modern/in-game directional compound combining the Wolayta exonym 'Welamo' with the English cardinal direction 'West'.

b_burji.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Burji oral traditions trace origins to the 16th century CE in Liban, with written documentation appearing in modern ethnographic and administrative records.

morphemes.translation: ethnonym and homeland south of Lake Chamo

b_burji.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym and toponym of the Highland East Cushitic-speaking Burji people in southern Ethiopia (also known natively as Daashi/Bambala).

b_yabelo.first_mention_attestation: First prominently documented in 20th-century written records (including the 1936 CE Italian occupation of southern Ethiopia); no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: town name in Borena Zone (also known as Obda)

b_yabelo.etymology_analysis: Oromo toponym (Yaabeelloo) for the administrative center of Borena Zone in southern Ethiopia.

b_dara-sharka.first_mention_attestation: The medieval Muslim principality of Dara is first attested in the 14th century CE in the Royal Chronicle of Emperor Amda Seyon I (c. 1332 CE) and by Arab historian al-Umari (c. 1340s CE) as one of the Seven States of Zeila; '-Sharka' is an in-game disambiguator. No documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: medieval Muslim principality east of Bale

b_dara-sharka.etymology_analysis: Compound of the medieval Muslim principality of Dara (part of the Zeila confederation in southeastern Ethiopia) with '-Sharka' as a game-level disambiguator.

b_abaya.first_mention_attestation: First documented in European written records in 1896 CE by Italian explorer Vittorio Bottego (who renamed it Lago Margherita); no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: Rift Valley lake name in southern Ethiopia

b_abaya.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of Lake Abaya, Ethiopia's second-largest lake, located in the Main Ethiopian Rift east of the Guge Mountains.

b_borama.first_mention_attestation: Modern town of Borama was founded in 1921 CE by Ughaz 'Elmi Warfa under the British Somaliland protectorate (while archaeological remains in the surrounding area date to the 12th–18th centuries CE); no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: deep holes, basins, or geological depressions/valleys

b_borama.etymology_analysis: From Somali 'booraan' (plural 'booraamo'), meaning a deep hole, basin, or valley, referring to the surrounding valleys ('place of valleys').

b_jam-jam.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; 'Jam-Jam' (Jemjem / Jamjamtu) is a local exonym and historical highland/awraja designation for the Guji Oromo in southern Ethiopia.

morphemes.translation: exonym for the Guji Oromo and Jamjam highland

b_jam-jam.etymology_analysis: Traditional exonym (Jamjam / Jamjamtu) applied by neighboring ethnic groups to the Guji Oromo of southern Ethiopia.

b_hadya.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written records in the 13th century CE (the Kebra Nagast, ch. 94, and a 1286/1287 CE reference in connection with Shewa) and in the 14th century CE chronicles of Emperor Amda Seyon I (1316/1317 CE) and al-Umari; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: medieval Muslim kingdom and Cushitic ethnonym in southern Ethiopia

b_hadya.etymology_analysis: Name of the medieval Hadiya Sultanate and Cushitic Hadiyya people in south-central Ethiopia (popularly linked in folk etymology to Arabic 'hadiyya', meaning 'gift').

b_ganz.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written records in the 1320s CE as an Islamic state allied against Emperor Amda Seyon I; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: medieval Ethiopian province north of Hadiya

b_ganz.etymology_analysis: Medieval Ethiopian principality and province (also known as Ganazo or Ganzo) located in the central Ethiopian highlands around modern Addis Ababa, north of Hadiya.

b_sharka.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written records in the 14th century CE in the Royal Chronicle of Emperor Amda Seyon I (r. 1314–1344 CE) and by Arab historians al-Umari and al-Maqrizi; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: medieval Muslim principality and province in eastern Arsi

b_sharka.etymology_analysis: Medieval Muslim principality (also transliterated Sharkha, Shirka, or Xarkhah) bordered by Hadiya, Dawaro, and Bale, identified with Širk in eastern Arsi.

b_munesa.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Munesa is a modern Oromia woreda in Arsi Zone (though 11th–13th century CE Islamic gravestones aged 1000–1270 CE were found near Lake Langano in the district).

morphemes.translation: district and forest name in Arsi Zone

b_munesa.etymology_analysis: Oromo toponym for the Munesa woreda and Munesa Forest in Arsi Zone, Great Rift Valley, Ethiopia.

b_kambata.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written records in the 15th century CE in the chronicles of Emperor Yeshaq I (r. 1413–1430 CE); no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: Cushitic ethnic group and historic kingdom around Mount Hambaricho

b_kambata.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym and toponym of the Highland East Cushitic-speaking Kambaata people and Kingdom of Kembata in south-central Ethiopia.

b_al-abwab.first_mention_attestation: First attested as al-Abwāb in Ibn Sulaym al-Aswani's Kitab Akhbar al-Nuba (c. 975 CE, preserved in al-Maqrizi's Khitat), and later in 13th–14th century CE Mamluk chronicles.
b_al-abwab.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Abwāb ('The Doors' or 'The Gates'), referring to the northernmost province of Alodia and later independent medieval Nubian kingdom.

b_shendi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; first documented in post-medieval Funj-era and 19th-century European traveler accounts.

morphemes.translation: riverbend 'lip' (Old Nubian shandi), 'ram/sheep' (Meroitic/Daju), or 'long winter' (Beja shanda)

b_shendi.etymology_analysis: Toponym of uncertain pre-Arabic origin; proposed etymologies include Old Nubian shandi ('lip', referring to the Nile bend), Meroitic/Daju ('ram/sheep'), and Beja shanda ('long winter').

b_keli.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern Sudanese settlement name near Shendi in River Nile State.

morphemes.translation: local Sudanese settlement name of uncertain etymology

b_keli.etymology_analysis: Local Sudanese settlement name in the Shendi reach of the Nile; exact linguistic origin unattested.

b_wad_hamid.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; post-medieval Sudanese Arabic patronymic settlement name.

eponym.details: Named after a post-867 CE Arabized Sudanese ancestor or local sheikh named Hamid (Arabic: Wad Ḥāmid, 'son of Hamid').

b_wad_hamid.etymology_analysis: Sudanese Arabic compound Wad Ḥāmid ('son/descendant of Hamid'), a typical post-medieval tribal/patronymic settlement name.

b_al-ghazali.first_mention_attestation: While the Makurian monastery in Wadi Abu Dom dates archaeologically to c. 680–720 CE, its modern Arabic name al-Ghazali is unattested in written sources <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: pertaining to gazelles (modern Sudanese site name)

b_al-ghazali.etymology_analysis: Modern Arabic name applied to the ruined medieval Makurian monastery in Wadi Abu Dom; its original medieval Nubian/Coptic name is not preserved as al-Ghazali.

b_atbara.first_mention_attestation: The modern form Atbara (ʿAṭbarah) is unattested <= 867 CE; Atbara is first recorded in post-medieval accounts (e.g., 1619 CE Ethiopian campaign), and the modern city grew as an Anglo-Egyptian railway hub after 1898 CE.
b_atbara.etymology_analysis: Named after the Atbarah River, an Arabicized adaptation of classical Astaboras (explained by Pliny the Elder as 'water coming from the shades below').

historical_names.name: Astaboras
historical_names.source: Strabo's Geographica (c. 20 BCE, citing Eratosthenes) and Pliny the Elder's Naturalis Historia (5.10, 77 CE)
historical_names.notes: The Atbarah River at whose confluence Atbara stands was known as Astaboras in Greco-Roman antiquity.

b_berber.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Ibn Sulaym al-Aswani's late 10th-century CE account (c. 975 CE, preserved in al-Maqrizi's Khitat) mentioning the road from Berber and al-Shunqayr to Sawakin and Badi'.
b_berber.etymology_analysis: Arabic Barbar (بربر), an ethnonymic toponym associated with the medieval Arabic designation Barābra for Nubian/eastern Nile populations.

b_al-bawga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern Sudanese town in Berber locality, River Nile State.

morphemes.translation: local riverine settlement name of uncertain etymology

b_al-bawga.etymology_analysis: Modern Sudanese Arabic toponym in the Berber reach of the Nile; no documented pre-867 attestation.

b_ed-damer.first_mention_attestation: Founded toward the end of the 15th century CE (c. 1500 CE) as a Sudanese Islamic center, later described by John Lewis Burckhardt in 1814 CE.
b_ed-damer.etymology_analysis: Arabic ad-Dāmar (الدامر), a late-15th-century Sudanese Islamic town near the Atbara-Nile confluence.

b_shunqayr.first_mention_attestation: First attested in writing as al-Shunqayr in Ibn Sulaym al-Aswani's c. 975 CE account (preserved in al-Maqrizi's Khitat), describing the gold-mining region east of the Berber–Abu Hamad Nile stretch.
b_shunqayr.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Shunqayr, corresponding to medieval Nubian Scienkur/Shenqir along the Nile between Berber and the Fourth Cataract.

b_old_dongola.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation of the retrofitted name 'Old Dongola' <= 867 CE; the 'Old' modifier was added after New Dongola (modern Dongola) was founded in 1812 CE, whereas the medieval Makurian capital was attested as Dunqulā (651–652 CE) and Tungul.

morphemes.translation: from Tungul (possibly from Old Nubian touŋ, 'to be secure', i.e. fortress)

b_old_dongola.etymology_analysis: Arabic Dunqulā (دنقلا), derived from Old Nubian Tungul (ⲧⲩⲛⲅⲩⲗ), possibly from touŋ ('to be secure', hence 'fortress'); 'Old' was added after New Dongola was founded in 1812 CE.

historical_names.name: Tungul
historical_names.source: 651–652 CE (early Arabic historiography of the Arab siege of Dunqulā by Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam and al-Baladhuri; Old Nubian Tungul)
historical_names.notes: The 'Old' modifier was retrofitted after New Dongola was founded in 1812 CE; the unmodified pre-867 CE base names are Tungul and Dunqulā.

historical_names.name: Dunqulā
historical_names.source: 651–652 CE (early Arabic historiography of the Arab siege of Dunqulā by Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam and al-Baladhuri; Old Nubian Tungul)
historical_names.notes: The 'Old' modifier was retrofitted after New Dongola was founded in 1812 CE; the unmodified pre-867 CE base names are Tungul and Dunqulā.

b_tumbus.first_mention_attestation: Although Tombos has New Kingdom Egyptian inscriptions (c. 1500 BCE), the modern Nubian name Tumbus/Tombos is unattested in written sources <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: Third Cataract island and settlement name of uncertain etymology

b_tumbus.etymology_analysis: Modern Nubian toponym (Tombos/Tumbus) at the Third Cataract; ancient Egyptian texts at the site do not preserve this name.
