b_kemna.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern Nubian/Arabic site name (variant of Kumma / Semna East, though placed in Dongola in-game).

morphemes.translation: local Nubian site name (variant of Kumma)

b_kemna.etymology_analysis: Variant of Kumma (Semna East), a modern Nubian/Arabic site name not attested in pre-867 written records.

b_dongola.first_mention_attestation: Modern Dongola (originally Urdu / New Dongola) was founded in 1812 CE by Mamluk refugees 80 km downstream from Old Dongola, borrowing the medieval city's name.

morphemes.translation: fortress / secure place (borrowed from Old Dongola)

b_dongola.etymology_analysis: Named after medieval Old Dongola (Old Nubian Tungul, Arabic Dunqulā) when Mamluk refugees established New Dongola downriver in 1812 CE.

b_debba.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; Al Dabbah (Ed Debba) appears in post-medieval Sudanese and 19th-century accounts.
b_debba.etymology_analysis: Arabic ad-Dabbah ('the sandy mound/hillock'), a post-medieval riverine town at the great bend of the Nile.

b_grnetti.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; local modern village name in the Meroë/Kabushiya area.

morphemes.translation: local settlement name near Meroë of uncertain etymology

b_grnetti.etymology_analysis: Modern local village name in the Meroë reach; no pre-867 written attestation.

historical_names.name: Meroë
historical_names.source: Herodotus's Histories (c. 450 BCE) and Meroitic royal inscriptions (capital of Kush from c. 590 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Serves as the in-game capital of c_meroe, near the ancient Kushite capital of Meroë (c. 590 BCE – 4th century CE).

historical_names.name: Medewi
historical_names.source: Herodotus's Histories (c. 450 BCE) and Meroitic royal inscriptions (capital of Kush from c. 590 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Serves as the in-game capital of c_meroe, near the ancient Kushite capital of Meroë (c. 590 BCE – 4th century CE).

b_tankasi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern Nubian name for an island and archaeological site near Merowe.

morphemes.translation: local Nile island and settlement name of uncertain etymology

b_tankasi.etymology_analysis: Modern Nubian island and settlement name in the Southern Dongola Reach; pre-867 name unattested.

b_kareima.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern Sudanese town adjacent to Jebel Barkal and ancient Napata.
b_kareima.etymology_analysis: Modern Arabic town name Karīma ('noble/generous'), founded near the ancient Kushite religious center of Napata.

historical_names.name: Napata
historical_names.source: Ancient Egyptian 18th Dynasty inscriptions (npt/npy, c. 15th century BCE) and classical Greek sources
historical_names.notes: Modern Karima is located immediately adjacent to Jebel Barkal and the ancient Kushite city of Napata.

b_nuri.first_mention_attestation: Although the Napatan royal necropolis at Nuri dates to c. 650–300 BCE, the modern Arabic/Nubian place name Nuri is unattested in written sources <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: modern site name near Jebel Barkal of uncertain etymology

b_nuri.etymology_analysis: Modern Sudanese site name for the ancient Napatan royal pyramid field; its ancient name is not preserved as Nuri.

b_diffar.first_mention_attestation: While the Makurian fortress at Ed-Diffar dates archaeologically to the 6th–14th centuries CE, the Arabic name Ed-Diffar is unattested in written sources <= 867 CE (first recorded in 19th-century traveler drawings).

morphemes.translation: local Dongola Reach fortress and settlement name

b_diffar.etymology_analysis: Modern Sudanese Arabic name for a medieval Makurian fortified enclosure in the Southern Dongola Reach.

b_sai.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Ancient Egyptian New Kingdom inscriptions (18th Dynasty, c. 1500 BCE) as Shaat (Šꜣꜥt) and in medieval Old Nubian/Christian Nubian sources as Zaē/Sai.

morphemes.translation: island fortress and bishopric name in Upper Nubia

b_sai.etymology_analysis: Continuous Nubian island toponym from Ancient Egyptian Šꜣꜥt through Old Nubian Zaē (ⲍⲁⲏ) to modern Saï.

b_delgo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern Nubian town in the Mahas/Abri-Delgo Reach of Northern State.

morphemes.translation: local Nubian settlement name in the Abri-Delgo Reach

b_delgo.etymology_analysis: Modern Nubian settlement name in Upper Nubia; no pre-867 written attestation.

b_kassi-markol.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern Nubian name for an early medieval fortified site near the Third Cataract.

morphemes.translation: local Third Cataract fortified site name

b_kassi-markol.etymology_analysis: Modern Nubian compound toponym for an archaeological fortified site in the Third Cataract region.

b_wadi_el-milk.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; post-medieval Arabic hydronym for the 560 km dry riverbed running to Al Dabbah.
b_wadi_el-milk.etymology_analysis: Arabic Wādī al-Malik (also rendered Wadi el-Milk), a major paleochannel and seasonal wadi in northern Sudan.

b_jebel_abu_negila.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern Sudanese Arabic hill/mountain name in the Bayuda/Wadi el-Milk region.
b_jebel_abu_negila.etymology_analysis: Sudanese Arabic oronym Jabal Abū Najīla ('mountain of Abu Negila').

b_bir_el-kai.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern Sudanese Arabic desert well name.
b_bir_el-kai.etymology_analysis: Sudanese Arabic well name Biʾr al-Kai in the desert steppe west of the Nile.

b_upper_milk.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern English geographical descriptor for the upper reach of Wadi el-Milk.
b_upper_milk.etymology_analysis: English geographic designation for the upper course of Wadi al-Malik (Wadi el-Milk).

b_semna.first_mention_attestation: The modern Arabic name Semna is unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; the Middle Kingdom Egyptian fortress (c. 1965–1839 BCE) bore the Egyptian name Sekhem-Khakaure.

morphemes.translation: modern site name at the Second Cataract gorge

b_semna.etymology_analysis: Modern Nubian/Arabic site name for the Middle Kingdom Egyptian fortress complex at the Semna Cataract.

historical_names.name: Sekhem-Khakaure
historical_names.source: Middle Kingdom Egyptian Semna stelae and dispatches of Senusret III (c. 1850 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Egyptian Middle Kingdom fortress name ('Powerful is Khakaure') before the modern name Semna.

b_akasha.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; although Old Nubian inscriptions and medieval monasteries were excavated at Akasha West, the modern name Akasha is post-medieval.

morphemes.translation: modern Nubian/Arabic village and hot-spring site name

b_akasha.etymology_analysis: Modern Sudanese Arabic name for the Batn el-Hajar settlement and hot springs (Hammam Akasha).

b_faras.first_mention_attestation: The Arabic form Faras is unattested <= 867 CE; pre-867 sources call the Nobadian capital Pachoras (Greek Pakhōras, Old Nubian Pakhōras).
b_faras.etymology_analysis: Arabic Faras, a phonetic adaptation of Greek/Old Nubian Pachoras (Ⲡⲁⲭⲱⲣⲁⲥ), the ancient capital of Nobatia.

historical_names.name: Pachoras
historical_names.source: Greco-Nubian and Coptic inscriptions from Faras (capital of Nobatia from c. 400 CE; cathedral founded 707 CE)
historical_names.notes: Known as Pachoras (Pakhōras) in late antiquity and the early medieval period prior to Arabic Faras.

historical_names.name: Pakhōras
historical_names.source: Greco-Nubian and Coptic inscriptions from Faras (capital of Nobatia from c. 400 CE; cathedral founded 707 CE)
historical_names.notes: Known as Pachoras (Pakhōras) in late antiquity and the early medieval period prior to Arabic Faras.

b_serra.first_mention_attestation: The modern name Serra is unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; Serra East was a Middle Kingdom Egyptian fortress (c. 1850 BCE) and later a medieval Christian town.
b_serra.etymology_analysis: Modern Lower Nubian settlement name covering Serra East and Serra West.

historical_names.name: Khesef-Medjayu
historical_names.source: Middle Kingdom Egyptian fortress list (Ramesseum Onomasticon, c. 1850–1700 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Serra East was the Middle Kingdom Egyptian fortress of Khesef-Medjayu ('Repelling the Medjay').

b_kalabsha.first_mention_attestation: The Arabic name Kalabsha (Bab al-Kalabsha) is unattested <= 867 CE; in Greco-Roman and early Nubian antiquity the site was called Talmis.

morphemes.translation: modern Arabic settlement name at ancient Talmis

b_kalabsha.etymology_analysis: Modern Arabic name Kalābsha (Bāb al-Kalābsha) for the Lower Nubian site of ancient Talmis.

historical_names.name: Talmis
historical_names.source: Roman-period Temple of Mandulis inscriptions (Augustus, c. 30 BCE–14 CE) and the 5th-century CE Silko inscription
historical_names.notes: Known in Greco-Roman and Nobadian antiquity as Talmis (Τάλμις) before the Arabic name Kalabsha.

b_sabagura.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern local name for a 6th-century CE fortified Lower Nubian town.

morphemes.translation: modern site name for a 6th-century fortified Lower Nubian town

b_sabagura.etymology_analysis: Modern local Nubian/Arabic site name for an early Christian fortified settlement in Lower Nubia.

b_qasr_ibrim.first_mention_attestation: The Arabic compound Qasr Ibrim is unattested <= 867 CE; pre-867 sources call the fortress-city Premnis/Primis (Greek/Latin), Prim (Coptic), or Silmi (Old Nubian).
b_qasr_ibrim.etymology_analysis: Arabic Qaṣr Ibrīm ('Fortress of Ibrim'), combining Arabic qaṣr with Ibrīm (adapted from Coptic Prim / Latin Primis).

historical_names.name: Primis
historical_names.source: Strabo's Geographica (17.1.54, c. 23 BCE) and Pliny the Elder's Naturalis Historia (6.181, 77 CE)
historical_names.notes: Attested as Premnis/Primis in Greco-Roman texts and Silmi in Old Nubian prior to Arabic Qasr Ibrim.

historical_names.name: Premnis
historical_names.source: Strabo's Geographica (17.1.54, c. 23 BCE) and Pliny the Elder's Naturalis Historia (6.181, 77 CE)
historical_names.notes: Attested as Premnis/Primis in Greco-Roman texts and Silmi in Old Nubian prior to Arabic Qasr Ibrim.

historical_names.name: Silmi
historical_names.source: Strabo's Geographica (17.1.54, c. 23 BCE) and Pliny the Elder's Naturalis Historia (6.181, 77 CE)
historical_names.notes: Attested as Premnis/Primis in Greco-Roman texts and Silmi in Old Nubian prior to Arabic Qasr Ibrim.

b_korosko.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; although the desert caravan route from this area was used in antiquity, the name Korosko is modern/19th-century.

morphemes.translation: Lower Nubian river settlement and caravan terminus name

b_korosko.etymology_analysis: Modern Nubian/Arabic riverine settlement name at the northern end of the Korosko desert road.

b_sheikh_dawud.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern Islamic saint-tomb name applied to a 6th-century Lower Nubian fortress site.

eponym.details: Named after a post-867 CE Muslim holy man or local sheikh (Sheikh Dawud) associated with the Lower Nubian site.

b_sheikh_dawud.etymology_analysis: Arabic Shaykh Dāwūd ('Sheikh David'), named after a local Islamic figure buried near the earlier Nobadian fortress.

b_qurta.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Cortia in Pliny the Elder's Naturalis Historia (6.181, 77 CE) and Corte in the 3rd-century CE Itinerarium Antonini, continuing as Coptic/Nubian Korta and Arabic Qurta.

morphemes.translation: Lower Nubian settlement and bishopric name

b_qurta.etymology_analysis: Continuous Lower Nubian toponym from Greco-Roman Cortia/Corte through medieval Nubian bishopric Korta to Arabic Qurṭa.

b_ikhmindi.first_mention_attestation: The modern form Ikhmindi is unattested <= 867 CE; the 6th-century fortified town (building inscription of King Tokiltoeton, c. 577 CE) was known as Mohondi in Coptic and Old Nubian.
b_ikhmindi.etymology_analysis: Arabicized modern name Ikhmindī, derived from medieval Nubian/Coptic Mohondi (ⲙⲱϩⲟⲛⲇⲓ).

historical_names.name: Mohondi
historical_names.source: Greek-Nubian building inscription of King Tokiltoeton at Ikhmindi (c. 577 CE) and Coptic/Old Nubian texts
historical_names.notes: Attested as Mohondi (Moondē) in medieval Coptic and Old Nubian texts before the modern form Ikhmindi.

b_sayala.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern Arabic name for a Lower Nubian archaeological site with A-Group, Roman, and Christian remains.

morphemes.translation: acacia tree (Acacia tortilis) or torrential stream

b_sayala.etymology_analysis: Arabic Sayāla, a common Sudanese/Egyptian Arabic toponym meaning 'acacia' or 'seasonal stream'.

b_abu_hammad.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; first recorded in 19th-century traveler accounts as a village named after a Muslim sheikh buried there.

eponym.details: Named after a post-867 CE Muslim sheikh (Abu Hamad) buried at the site, whose tomb served as a sacred landmark for desert caravans.

b_abu_hammad.etymology_analysis: Arabic Abū Ḥamad ('father of Hamad'), named after a local Islamic saint buried at the great Nile bend.

b_korosko_road.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; 19th-century English designation for the Nubian Desert caravan route between Korosko and Abu Hamad.
b_korosko_road.etymology_analysis: 19th-century English geographical name for the desert caravan trail connecting Korosko to Abu Hamad.

b_al-hajar_nubia.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern Arabic topographic name ('the stone/rock') with an in-game regional disambiguator.
b_al-hajar_nubia.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Ḥajar ('the stone/rock outcrop', cf. Hagar el-Merwa / Hagar el-Beida near Abu Hamad) with the disambiguator 'Nubia'.

b_kurgus.first_mention_attestation: Although Kurgus contains New Kingdom Egyptian boundary stelae (c. 1500 BCE) and a Christian fort (c. 600–1500 CE), the Nubian name Kurgus is unattested in written sources <= 867 CE.
b_kurgus.etymology_analysis: Modern Nubian toponym meaning 'yellow', applied to the Nile-side site near Hagar el-Merwa.

b_tarfaya.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern Arabic name for a medieval fortified site in the Fourth Cataract / Abu Hamad region.
b_tarfaya.etymology_analysis: Arabic Ṭarfāya ('tamarisk'), local Sudanese site name in the Fourth Cataract / Kurgus reach.

b_shemkhiya.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern Sudanese Arabic name for a settlement at the upstream end of the Fourth Cataract.

morphemes.translation: Fourth Cataract settlement and fortified site name

b_shemkhiya.etymology_analysis: Modern Sudanese Arabic settlement name in the Fourth Cataract region, often associated with the medieval Makurian bishopric of Scienkur/Shenqir.

b_redab.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern local name for a medieval fortified site in the Fourth Cataract region.
b_redab.etymology_analysis: Modern local Sudanese name for a medieval Nubian fortified site in the Fourth Cataract / Shamir region.

b_kuweib.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; although the site (Umm Kuweib) dates archaeologically to Late Antiquity (5th–6th centuries CE), the Arabic name Kuweib is modern.
b_kuweib.etymology_analysis: Modern Sudanese Arabic name (shortened from Umm Kuweib) for a late antique / early medieval fortified site in Upper Nubia.

b_soba.first_mention_attestation: 891 CE (al-Ya'qubi, Kitab al-Buldan, first written mention of Soba as the capital of the Kingdom of Alodia)
b_soba.etymology_analysis: Known in medieval Arabic as Sūbah (سوبة) and in Old Nubian as Sōba. Although archaeological remains at Soba date from the 5th–6th centuries CE and the Kingdom of Alodia is attested in 569 CE, the city name Soba itself is first attested in writing by al-Ya'qubi in 891 CE, after the 867 CE baseline.

b_geili.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern Sudanese village and archaeological site north of Khartoum documented in 20th-century CE excavations
b_geili.etymology_analysis: Modern Sudanese Arabic place-name (al-Jaylī / Geili) north of Khartoum near the Sixth Cataract, known archaeologically for Neolithic, Meroitic, and 16th-century CE Christian burials, but unattested in written sources <= 867 CE.

b_kadero.first_mention_attestation: 1955 CE (first documented archaeologically by H. N. Chittick; excavated 1972–2003 CE by Lech Krzyżaniak)
b_kadero.etymology_analysis: Modern Sudanese locality and major Neolithic pastoralist site northeast of Khartoum on the east bank of the Nile, first documented in 1955 CE and unattested in written records <= 867 CE.

b_alti.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern town in Al Jazirah State, Sudan
b_alti.etymology_analysis: Modern Sudanese settlement in Al Jazirah State south of Khartoum; no pre-867 CE written attestation exists.

b_kamlin.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern town and district (Al Kamlin) in Al Jazirah State, Sudan
b_kamlin.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Kāmlīn (الكاملين), a town and administrative district in Al Jazirah State on the Blue Nile; unattested in written records <= 867 CE.

b_el-eleila.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern settlement in central Sudan
b_el-eleila.etymology_analysis: Sudanese Arabic toponym with definite article al-/el- and diminutive pattern; unattested in written sources <= 867 CE.

b_abu_geili.first_mention_attestation: 1914 CE (excavated and documented by O. G. S. Crawford for Sir Henry Wellcome's Sudan expedition)
b_abu_geili.etymology_analysis: Modern Sudanese Arabic place-name on the Blue Nile near Sennar; although the site contains Meroitic and Funj-period remains, the name Abu Geili is first documented in 20th-century CE archaeological work (1914 CE).

b_basharga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern settlement (Beshagra / Basharga) in Al Jazirah State, Sudan
b_basharga.etymology_analysis: Modern Sudanese settlement in Al Jazirah State; unattested in written records <= 867 CE.

b_geteina.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern town (El Geteina / Al Qutaynah) in White Nile State, Sudan
b_geteina.etymology_analysis: From Sudanese Arabic al-Quṭaynah (القطينة), a town on the White Nile south of Khartoum; unattested in written sources <= 867 CE.

b_arbaji.first_mention_attestation: 1474 CE (recorded foundation of Arbaji on the Blue Nile by Arab settlers; later mentioned in Funj Chronicle and Ludolphus)
b_arbaji.etymology_analysis: Town on the left bank of the Blue Nile in Al Jazirah, Sudan, recorded as founded in 1474 CE by Arab settlers during the late Alodian period; unattested <= 867 CE.

b_um_sunt.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern settlement (Um Sunt) in Al Jazirah State, Sudan
b_um_sunt.etymology_analysis: Sudanese Arabic toponym Umm Sunṭ meaning 'place of acacia trees', referring to a settlement in Greater Madani, Al Jazirah State; unattested <= 867 CE.

b_saqadi.first_mention_attestation: 1951 CE (documented in Wellcome Excavations in the Sudan, Vol. III by Frank Addison, following early 20th-century CE fieldwork)
b_saqadi.etymology_analysis: Archaeological site (Jebel Saqadi) in southern Gezira containing a Meroitic-era settlement, the southernmost known Nubian church, and Funj-period remains, but the name Saqadi is only documented in 20th-century CE surveys.

b_naga.first_mention_attestation: 1822 CE (documented as Naqa / Naga'a by European traveler Frédéric Cailliaud; modern Arabic an-Naq'ah)
b_naga.etymology_analysis: From Sudanese Arabic an-Naqʿah (النقعة), the modern name of the ruined Kushite city in the Butana. While the ancient city dates back to the Meroitic period and was known in Meroitic as Tolakate / Tolkte, the Arabic name Naqa/Naga is post-867 CE.

historical_names.name: Tolakate
historical_names.source: c. 200 BCE–1st century CE Meroitic inscriptions (including 'Apedemak of Tolkte' at Musawwarat es-Sufra)
historical_names.notes: Meroitic city name Tolakate / Tolkte (Egyptian twjlkt) attested before 867 CE; replaced by Arabic an-Naq'ah (Naqa/Naga).

historical_names.name: Tolkte
historical_names.source: c. 200 BCE–1st century CE Meroitic inscriptions (including 'Apedemak of Tolkte' at Musawwarat es-Sufra)
historical_names.notes: Meroitic city name Tolakate / Tolkte (Egyptian twjlkt) attested before 867 CE; replaced by Arabic an-Naq'ah (Naqa/Naga).

b_basa.first_mention_attestation: 1907 CE (excavated and documented by Francis Llewellyn Griffith as Basa / Jabal Basa)

morphemes.translation: village and temple site in Butana

b_basa.etymology_analysis: Modern village (Basa / Jabal Basa) in the Butana steppe near a ruined Meroitic temple built by Amanikhabale; the modern toponym Basa is unattested <= 867 CE.

b_umm_usuda.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern Arabic name for a Meroitic archaeological site and hafir in the Butana documented in 20th-century CE surveys

morphemes.translation: lions (plural of asad, referring to Meroitic lion sculptures)

b_umm_usuda.etymology_analysis: Modern Sudanese Arabic name ('Mother of Lions') given to a Meroitic site in the Butana featuring a hafir guarded by lion sculptures and Meroitic stela REM 0045 (1st century CE); the Arabic name itself is unattested <= 867 CE.

b_jebel_geili.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern Arabic name (Jebel Geili / Gebel Qeili) documented in 20th-century CE archaeological surveys
b_jebel_geili.etymology_analysis: Sudanese Arabic oronym meaning 'Mount Geili', a granite outcrop east of Khartoum famous for the 1st-century CE Meroitic rock carving of King Shorkaror; the Arabic name Jebel Geili is unattested <= 867 CE.

b_ushara.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern settlement/district (Al-Ushara / El Ushara) in Khartoum, Sudan
b_ushara.etymology_analysis: Modern Sudanese Arabic place-name (al-ʿUshārah) in the Khartoum/Nile region; unattested in written records <= 867 CE.

b_shaheinab.first_mention_attestation: 1949 CE (excavated and published by A. J. Arkell as Esh Shaheinab)
b_shaheinab.etymology_analysis: Modern Sudanese Arabic place-name (Esh Shaheinab) 50 km north of Omdurman, famous for its Neolithic archaeological site first excavated by A. J. Arkell in 1949 CE; unattested <= 867 CE.

b_fazughli.first_mention_attestation: 1622 CE (mentioned in Pedro Páez's History of Ethiopia; Kingdom of Fazughli c. 1500–1685 CE)

morphemes.translation: Fazughli (borderland province and kingdom on the Blue Nile)

b_fazughli.etymology_analysis: Historical province and precolonial kingdom (Arabic Fāzūghlī فازوغلي) on the Sudan–Ethiopia borderland along the Blue Nile, attested from early modern sources (e.g., Pedro Páez 1622 CE) and conquered by Sennar in 1685 CE; unattested <= 867 CE.

b_al-rusayrisi.first_mention_attestation: 1829 CE (mentioned in Lord Prudhoe's travel diary while traveling in Sennar)

morphemes.translation: Er Roseires (diminutive toponym on the Blue Nile)

b_al-rusayrisi.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Rūṣayriṣ (الروصيرص, anglicized Er Roseires), a town on the Blue Nile in eastern Sudan first documented in 1829 CE by Lord Prudhoe.

b_fazughli_east.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern directional subdivision of Fazughli (attested from 1622 CE)
b_fazughli_east.etymology_analysis: Modern English directional subdivision of Fazughli (Arabic Fāzūghlī), which itself is unattested <= 867 CE.

b_gumuz_north.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern directional subdivision named after the Gumuz people of the Sudan–Ethiopia borderlands
b_gumuz_north.etymology_analysis: Modern directional subdivision named after the Gumuz, a Nilo-Saharan-speaking people of western Ethiopia and southeastern Sudan (historically grouped under the exonym Shanqella in 18th-century CE accounts); unattested <= 867 CE.

b_gumuz_west.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern directional subdivision named after the Gumuz people of the Sudan–Ethiopia borderlands
b_gumuz_west.etymology_analysis: Modern directional subdivision named after the Gumuz people of the Sudan–Ethiopia borderlands; unattested <= 867 CE.

b_gumuz_south.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern directional subdivision named after the Gumuz people of the Sudan–Ethiopia borderlands
b_gumuz_south.etymology_analysis: Modern directional subdivision named after the Gumuz people of the Sudan–Ethiopia borderlands; unattested <= 867 CE.

b_sennar.first_mention_attestation: 1504 CE (foundation of Sennar by Funj ruler Amara Dunqas as capital of the Funj Sultanate)
b_sennar.etymology_analysis: Founded in 1504 CE by Amara Dunqas as the capital of the Funj Sultanate (Sultanate of Sennar). Although a Meroitic trading station existed in the vicinity, the name Sennar (Sannār / سنار) is attested only from 1504 CE onward.

b_jebel_moya.first_mention_attestation: 1911 CE (first excavated and documented by Sir Henry Wellcome, 1911–1914 CE)

morphemes.translation: water (referring to springs/aquifer at the massif)

b_jebel_moya.etymology_analysis: Sudanese Arabic oronym meaning 'Mountain of Water', referring to the granite massif in southern Gezira whose underground aquifer provides freshwater springs; although used as a pastoralist cemetery from 5000 BCE–500 CE, the Arabic name Jebel Moya is first documented in 20th-century CE archaeology (1911 CE).

b_singa.first_mention_attestation: 1924 CE (documented in colonial-era Blue Nile Province records with the discovery of the Singa Skull)
b_singa.etymology_analysis: Modern town (Sinja / Singa, سنجة) on the west bank of the Blue Nile in Sennar State, Sudan, known for the 1924 CE discovery of the Pleistocene Singa Skull; unattested in written records <= 867 CE.

b_renk.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern town on the eastern bank of the White Nile in Upper Nile, South Sudan

morphemes.translation: modern town on the White Nile

b_renk.etymology_analysis: Modern town on the east bank of the White Nile in Upper Nile State, South Sudan; unattested in written records <= 867 CE.

b_kosti.first_mention_attestation: 1899 CE (founded shortly after 1899 CE by Greek merchant Konstantinos 'Kostas' Mourikis)

eponym.details: Named after Konstantinos 'Kostas' Mourikis (1867–1937 CE), a Greek merchant who established a trading store on the White Nile there shortly after 1899 CE.

b_kosti.etymology_analysis: From Greek personal name Kōstas (diminutive of Konstantinos), adapted into Sudanese Arabic as Kūstī (كوستي); founded shortly after 1899 CE by Greek trader Konstantinos 'Kostas' Mourikis.

b_tagali.first_mention_attestation: c. 1750 CE (scholarly dating of the Kingdom of Taqali in the Nuba Mountains, though oral traditions place its origin in the early 16th century CE)

morphemes.translation: Tagale people and Nuba Mountains kingdom

b_tagali.etymology_analysis: From the Tagale people of the Taqali Massif in the Nuba Mountains, Kordofan. The Kingdom of Taqali is dated by scholars to c. 1750–1780 CE (or early 16th century CE in oral tradition), well after 867 CE.

b_tagali_south.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern directional subdivision of Tagali (Kingdom of Taqali, c. 1750 CE)
b_tagali_south.etymology_analysis: Modern English directional subdivision of Tagali (Kingdom of Taqali in the Nuba Mountains); unattested <= 867 CE.
